sentences.text: This animal possessed an incredibly deep and robust skull equipped with long teeth featuring compressed crowns. It reached a total length of around 4 meters.
Some researchers describe the Baru skull as altirostral, distinguishing it from the platyrostral snout shape found in generalist crocodilians like Paludirex, Kambara, and Australosuchus.
The name Baru comes from a figure in the Dreamtime of the East Arnhem Region.
The genus Baru was first described by Willis and colleagues in 1990, when the species B. darrowi was named.
The holotype of B. darrowi is a partial rostrum collected from Bullock Creek.
Fossils of Baru have been found in the Northern Territory and Queensland.
Baru is generally interpreted as a semi-aquatic ambush hunter that inhabited shallower waters than modern crocodiles.
The bite of Baru was thought to be powerful enough to kill large mammals up to 300 kg.
The second premaxillary tooth of Baru was gradually reduced and lost entirely as the animal aged.
Baru is now typically classified as a derived mekosuchine related to the semi-aquatic Paludirex.

A 2018 study by Lee and Yates found Baru claded with Pallimnarchus and Kalthifrons as a sister group to dwarf mekosuchines, while a recent study by Ristevski et al. grouped Baru with Paludirex and Quinkana, placing Kalthifrons as a more basal taxon.
Ultrastenos is now considered closer to Mekosuchus and Trilophosuchus.
Fossils of Baru date from the Late Oligocene to the Late Miocene, though the fossil range extends from the Late Oligocene to the Middle Miocene.
The species Baru huberi and Baru wickeni are older and were found in the Etadunna Formation dating to the Late Oligocene in Queensland.
Baru went extinct during the Late Miocene due to climate changes.
It is hypothesized that a pulse of aridification destroyed the habitat preferred by Baru.
It is debated whether Baru's teeth should be classified as ziphodont due to insufficient development of serrations compared to true ziphodont teeth like those of Quinkana.
Yates (2017) and later studies established that "Baru" huberi is not a species of Baru but belongs to the genus Ultrastenos.
There is currently no fossil evidence linking Late Miocene Baru iylwenpeny to its likely Late Oligocene divergence time.
